newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, Russia strike deal to liberalise steel trade.
newsitem.headline: EU, Russia strike deal to liberalise steel trade.

text.p: The European Commission on Tuesday announced a deal with Moscow that will allow Russia gradually to increase its steel exports to the European Union to the end of 2001, when free trade will be introduced.

The agreement, negotiated last week in Moscow, paves the way for full liberalisation of trade in steel between Russia and the 15-nation European Union. Russia has no restrictions on such imports from the EU.
This would be linked to Russia developing "normal competitive condititions" concerning competition policy, state aid and environmental protection in the steel sector.

"This agreement shows Europe's commitment to open markets and provides a strong incentive to Russia to build its steel sector firmly on the principles of fair trade, rigorous competition and a clean environment," EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said.
"This will benefit industry and consumers on both sides," he said in a statement. The EU reached a similar market-opening accord with Ukraine on March 20.

Today, only 14 percent of the EU market for Russian and Ukrainian steel exports is covered by quotas, "but nonetheless we want to open it up completely," EU trade spokesman Peter Guilford told reporters.
There would be a major review of the agreement after two and a half years to assess what progress had been made.

Asked about the consequences of the agreement for European steel makers, European Commission trade official Salvatore Salerno said he did not expect any major impact. "So all things being equal our steel sector can cope," he said.
The Russia-EU accord would introduce a special regime to avert the risk of anti-dumping complaints from industry. "We are trying to reduce trade frictions with Russia," Salerno said.

Under the accord, EU quotas on Russian steel will be raised for most products by 10 percent in 1997, to a total of 841,224 tonnes. They will increase a further five percent in 1998 and 2.5 percent more each year until the end of 2001.
"This process could happen even earlier depending on when Russia applies competition, state aid and environmental disciplines compatible with those in the EU," a statement from the EU executive said.
The agreement would be reviewed if Russia joins the World Trade Organisation (WTO) before 2001.
The deal with Russia adjusts the quotas to increase limits for coils and certain long products that Russia can export and cut others that it cannot fully use, the Commission said.
The accord will be submitted to EU member states and the Russian government for approval and should enter into force in October.
EU negotiators also have a mandate to strike a similar agreement with Kazakhstan, the third largest producer among former Soviet republics which has a substantial export potential.

EU imports of iron and steel products from the group of former Soviet republics in the Commonwealth of Independent States rose to 7.49 million tonnes in 1995 from 2.76 million in 1993. "This reflects the openness of the Community steel market," the Commission said.
Russia accounts for some 80 percent of total EU steel and iron imports from the CIS, which groups 12 ex-Soviet republics.
In contrast, EU exports to Russia have virtually disappeared, largely due to the collapse in domestic consumption following the demise of the Soviet Union.
